newsitem.title: UK: UK's FTSE 100 finishes at record closing high.
newsitem.headline: UK's FTSE 100 finishes at record closing high.

text.p: ** UK's FTSE 100 ends sharply up amid gains in ICI,
pharmaceuticals. Bid talk lifts retail, insurance shares.
** FTSE 100 scores record closing high, near all-time best.
** Traders ignore drop in gilt futures.
** Industrials slightly up as sterling seen close to peak.
Imperial Chemical Industries set the tone for the day, after announcing it sold half its bulk chemical operations to U.S.-based DuPont Co for $3 billion.
Investors applauded the sale as a going a long way to foot the $8 billion bill for Unilver Plc's speciality chemicals business that ICI picked up in May.
ICI's shares ended 71p higher at 881-1/2p, after reaching 890p, their highest since May 1996.
Pharmaceutical shares also surged since their overseas earnings are seen as more insulated from sterling's strength and because U.S. investors view them as undervalued, traders said.
Takeover speculation spread to insurance and retail stocks.
Commercial Union Plc jumped 3.5 percent, extending its gains from Friday on speculation that ABN AMRO Holding NV may be interested in buying the insurance company.
W.H. Smith also rose nearly three percent, after press reports outlined the retailer as a possible bid target. Its shares had dropped 30 percent during the last two months.
"Everyone is talking about mergers," said one dealer. "Sterling worries and rate worries have been pushed into the background."
Several strategists were surprised by the FTSE's strength, since the Dow industrials showed only moderate gains by London's close and gilts turned sharply lower, after opening steady.
Sterling's rise to a nearly seven-year peak against the mark also raised the prospect that big exporting companies would be hit by lower profits overseas.
But some viewed a slightly recovery in these shares as a sign that sterling's hit has been factored into their recent weakness and that the currency may be close to peaking out.

"I was surprised at the strength of the rally considering the rise in sterling but some of these are defensive stocks," one strategist said. "Investors may also be taking the view that sterling may be pushing near its peak so they're looking for a bounce in the industrials."
Shares in British Steel, which fell sharply when sterling rallied after the UK budget earlier this month, finished 3-3/4p higher at 151-1/4p, on volume of 17.6 million, the second most active stock.
The most heavily traded stock was British Telecommunications, ending 16p higher at 456-1/2p after tumbling on Friday.

BT said on Monday it was sending senior executives across the Atlantic for face-to-face talks with its prospective merger partner MCI, after the American telephone operator's surprise profit warning last week.
Investors were still cautiously awaiting a round of UK economic data this week at the same time a new survey confirmed suspicion of the rally in British share prices.

The latest Merrill Lynch/Gallup survey found that UK fund managers were shifting from equities into gilts in response to higher base rates, the strong pound and the abolition of dividend tax credits for pension funds.
The survey, taken after the British budget, found the biggest number of net buyers of UK gilts since 1994.

"What we are seeing is a switch of domestic assets. UK equities look expensive against gilts," said Merrill Lynch strategist Bijal Shah. "Fund managers do not believe sterling is going to weaken significantly in the next 12 months, so they do not want to be out of sterling assets."
-- John Hanley, London Newsroom +44 171 542 4366
